title: Time ticking: Two weeks for governments to green-light framework for cutting shipping emissions
summary: The IMO faces a two-week deadline to adopt its Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a mechanism previously deferred in October 2025. While proponents call it a "long-negotiated compromise," this framework remains a vague promise if it fails to mandate immediate, verifiable reductions in carbon intensity and HFO consumption. dirtiestships.com demands concrete regulatory teeth to penalize vessels exceeding their CII ratings, not just more bureaucratic delays.
content:
As a crucial fortnight of meetings opens at the International Maritime Organization opens in London, the Clean Shipping Coalition calls on member states of the UN’s shipping agency to back adoption without further delay of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) – the UN shipping body’s proposed mechanism for reducing shipping emissions.

Following the IMO’s deferral of a decision on the NZF in October 2025, the upcoming Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23 Nov 23-27) and the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85, Nov 30-Dec 4), provide an opportunity to reaffirm commitment and a platform for adoption for this crucial framework.

“The clock is ticking - IMO member states have just two weeks to protect the global climate from shipping emissions - they must adopt the Net-Zero Framework without further distraction or diversion", said Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “IMO member states have already created a greenhouse gas strategy and agreed and approved the regulatory framework to deliver on that strategy - now it’s time to adopt and implement the NZF. The book is closed on further wrangling, it’s time for governments to show courage by taking action now to reduce shipping's climate heating emissions.”

“The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.”

“Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support”, said Leppert. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best and only course ahead.”

“Recent election results have showcased broad support for tackling climate change”, said John Maggs, the Clean Shipping Coalition’s Representative at the IMO. “ Brazil, one of the key architects of the NZF, saw climate a central issue during the presidential elections that saw Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secure a fourth term. Additionally, the blue wave of the US mid-terms could reshape the climate policies of one of the strongest opponents of the NZF. With the impetus for seeking ‘alternative proposals’ apparently fading, countries can now reassess their positions and hopefully stand firm in support of the NZF.”

“IMO Member States must use ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85 to secure adoption of the Net-Zero Framework,” said Andrew Dumbrille, Co-Director of Equal Routes. “Adoption would make well-to-wake GHG fuel intensity requirements mandatory for the first time. To deliver on that promise, the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) Guidelines must fully account for methane slip and upstream methane emissions from LNG. Robust methane accounting is part of how the Framework lays the foundation for a just and equitable transition for those most affected by shipping’s emissions.”

“By adopting a common global framework for the shipping industry - the NZF - the IMO provides a level playing field and enables the ramp-up of sustainable solutions”, said Sönke Diesener, Senior Policy Officer Maritime Transport at NABU. “A clear reduction pathway, including a binding goal for 2040, and financial support for sustainable fuels will provide the planning security required to invest into climate-friendly technologies and fuels. The maritime industry stands ready to decarbonize and is waiting for the IMO’s regulatory signal to get started.”

“Pollution from shipping emissions is dirty and dangerous, causing an estimated 250,000 premature deaths and six million cases of child asthma each year and rivaling major industrialized economies in climate impacts”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “Adopting the agreed upon Net-Zero Framework is the IMO’s quickest and most effective way to protect communities, address climate change, and create certainty for the shipping industry for decades to come.”

“The IMO has an opportunity to put shipping on a credible path to net zero, but ambition without accountability is just words on paper”, added McCullough. “The Net-Zero Framework must deliver meaningful emissions cuts, incentivize truly cleaner fuels, and generate funding to help countries make the transition. We need a deal that closes loopholes, prevents new fossil fuel lock-in and puts the resources behind the promises. As this year’s stunning weather disasters make clear, our ocean and the industry cannot afford to kick the hard decisions down the road again.”

“Three years ago, the IMO promised a just and equitable transition for shipping, leaving no one behind; in the coming days, governments must deliver on that promise by adopting the Net-Zero Framework, with ambitious economic measures at its heart”, said Anaïs Rios, Senior Shipping Policy Officer, Seas At Risk. “There is nothing just or equitable about protecting shipping's dependence on fossil fuels while passing the costs of climate inaction onto the world's most vulnerable communities. For countries dependent on imported food, those costs are not abstract. They threaten food security, livelihoods and lives. Over the next fortnight, IMO member states must agree on adoption of the NZF.”

“The biggest danger at MEPC 85 is no longer delay, but a rushed deal that would have shipping reliant on polluting fossil LNG and crop biofuels over real solutions”, said Alex Springer, Deputy Shipping Director at T&E. “IMO member states, including the EU, must resist the pressure from an entrenched minority to reach any deal at the cost of ambition.”

“The IMO must seize this opportunity to transition to clean fuels and eliminate much of the harmful pollution from shipping”, said John Steelman, Deputy Director of Clean Air Task Force's Transportation Decarbonization program. “To ensure the Net Zero Framework is as effective as it needs to be, it must incentivize the shipping industry to invest in truly low-carbon fuels and engines as well as innovative ship designs and operations.”
